nodes.label: ADR 0005: compacting the data branch by re-orphaning under a lease
nodes.rationale: Status accepted. Git and github transports commit every mutation (195 commits for ~100 messages in two live runs), so the tree stays small but history grows forever. Two harms: joining costs more forever because initialise fetches every reachable object, and the repository grows without bound until it hits the host size limit and stops accepting pushes, which ends the workspace.

nodes.label: Compaction (re-orphaning the data branch)
nodes.rationale: Periodically replace the data branch with a single parentless commit holding the branch's current tree, published with a compare-and-swap force-push. Reusing the existing tree object means content is preserved bit for bit rather than rebuilt, so compaction cannot corrupt or drop a message by construction. Measured on a 201-commit history: 803 objects/588K/depth 201 uncompacted versus 10 objects/160K/depth 1 compacted, against a remote that had NOT been garbage collected, which is the only case that matters because no client can make GitHub run a gc.

nodes.label: The data branch
nodes.rationale: The git branch every mutation is committed to. A send is a commit, the response is a commit, and the delete that acknowledges delivery is a third.

nodes.label: git commit-tree (parentless commit)
nodes.rationale: commit-tree with no -p produces a commit with no parents, which is what makes the result an orphan. Three plumbing commands total, touching neither the working tree nor the index.

nodes.label: Explicit-value --force-with-lease=<branch>:<commit>
nodes.rationale: The lease must take an explicit expected value, never the bare --force-with-lease. The bare form leases against the remote-tracking ref, which sync() refreshes constantly; a poll landing between snapshot and push would silently update origin/<branch>, make the lease agree with itself, and turn the compare-and-swap into an unconditional force-push. This is the entire safety argument and must not be simplified away. Protect it with a test that would have caught its absence, not one that covers its presence.

nodes.label: Any peer may compact, no election
nodes.rationale: The lease makes concurrent attempts safe: one wins, the others are rejected against a tip already compacted by somebody else. A rejected compaction is not retried and not an error; it is logged at debug and dropped, because the work it wanted done is done.

nodes.label: Flush lock serialisation of compaction
nodes.rationale: Compaction runs inside the existing flush lock, after a successful flush, so it cannot interleave with applyBatch in our own process. The flush lock is the mechanism that already serialises writes.

nodes.label: compactAfterCommits config field
nodes.rationale: Trigger is local history depth via git rev-list --count HEAD, a local read. Defaults to 500 with 0 to disable, keeping compaction roughly two orders of magnitude rarer than the pushRetries budget of 5 that absorbs its collisions.

nodes.label: pushRetries budget
nodes.rationale: Budget of 5 retries that absorbs collisions caused by compaction losing or winning a race.

nodes.label: Refused compaction waits a full threshold
nodes.rationale: A lost lease means somebody else is compacting; a branch protected against force-pushes will refuse the next attempt too. Without the floor, either case spends a wasted push on every flush, a throughput regression paid forever in exchange for nothing.

nodes.label: sync() fetch plus reset --hard
nodes.rationale: sync() is already git fetch origin <branch> followed by git reset --hard origin/<branch>, and a hard reset adopts an unrelated history as readily as a descendant one. The + in the refspec +refs/heads/*:refs/remotes/origin/* lets the non-fast-forward remote-tracking update through, so every peer picks up a rewritten branch through the code path it already runs every five seconds. This is why peers need no new code to survive compaction.

nodes.label: initialise (git init plus fetch)
nodes.rationale: Transfers every object reachable from the branch tip. Since the 0.2.5 working-tree ownership lock, a second runtime on one machine and every ddrop connect clone separately into <workDir>.peers/ and pay that cost again.

nodes.label: applyBatch replay loop
nodes.rationale: Treats a compaction it lost a race to exactly as any other lost race: reset to the remote, replay the batch, push again. Compaction adds a new cause for a code path that already exists, not a new code path.

nodes.label: isNonFastForward rejection matcher
nodes.rationale: Already matches both the 'stale info' and 'fetch first' rejection messages compaction produces.

nodes.label: ensureClone memoised-failure clearing
nodes.rationale: When a peer's fetch fails because the host stopped serving objects the branch no longer reaches, the error is retryable, ensureClone clears its memoised failure, and the next attempt succeeds against the new tip.

nodes.label: Two-peer lab verification of the four safety properties
nodes.rationale: Verified against real git rather than reasoned about, because the failure mode of getting this wrong is silent message loss, the exact class of defect that has already bitten this project twice. Results: tree preserved (depth 31 to 1, identical tree object, 30 of 30 messages); an existing peer recovered unaided through plain fetch plus reset --hard; a concurrent writer was protected (lease rejected with stale info); a peer mid-flush was rejected 'fetch first' and the existing replay loop re-pushed intact.

nodes.label: Rejected: shallow fetch (--depth=1)
nodes.rationale: Not a strawman: tested and works, a shallow peer joined a 201-commit remote at 124K, pushed back successfully and stayed shallow across an ordinary sync, needing no force-push. Rejected as THE answer because it fixes only the join cost while the host repository still grows forever. Complementary rather than alternative, and it has an unmeasured tail: a shallow peer accumulates every commit made after it joined and drifts back unless it re-shallows.

nodes.label: Rejected: delete and recreate the branch
nodes.rationale: Strictly worse than a leased force-push: there is a window in which the branch does not exist, and any peer calling initialise in that window takes the create-orphan path and races to publish a competing branch.

nodes.label: Rejected: epoch scheme (a branch per generation)
nodes.rationale: Solves the same problem with more moving parts, and every reader has to discover which epoch is current before it can read anything. The force-push is renamed into a branch deletion rather than avoided.

nodes.label: Rejected: rewriting history with filter-branch or filter-repo
nodes.rationale: Same force-push, same lease requirement, far slower, and pointless: nothing needs the intermediate commits rewritten, only discarded.

nodes.label: Commit history as the only record a message existed
nodes.rationale: Delivery is delete-as-acknowledgement, so the data branch's commit log is the sole place a delivered message survives. Nothing reads it and no feature depends on it, so nothing breaks, but it forecloses an accidental audit trail. That supports the backlog position that an audit story needs designing deliberately: commit history is metadata the encryption exists to protect and should not become a feature by default. Also, git log stops being a hand-debugging tool for a workspace.

nodes.label: Nobody's disk shrinks on its own
nodes.rationale: An existing peer keeps old objects until it runs git gc; measured, a peer sat at 3.7M and fell to 136K only after reflog expire --expire=now --all plus gc --prune=now. The host keeps them until its own gc, which cannot be triggered. Compaction fixes what a new peer pays, immediately, not what an old peer already holds.

nodes.label: Compaction degrades gracefully
nodes.rationale: If the branch is force-push protected or the host refuses the lease, compaction fails, the failure is logged, messages keep flowing, and history keeps growing as today. It can never take a workspace down; it can only fail to help.

hyperedges.label: Compaction survives races because existing code paths already handle it
